summary: Round 2. All six round-1 findings verified fixed: F1 the barrier case does force overlap and asserts one winner plus a whole body; F2 list is now one call/one page/one request with a checked IOException per page and an Optional resume point, which is exactly what CountingBinStore and M1.3b's LIST ceiling need; F3 seeks from the later of prefix and startAfter, with a below-prefix case that bites; F4 readFully enforces length and both write paths call it; F5 clamps, with the equivalent mutant disclosed rather than hidden; F6 CostTable is a Capabilities component from v1. No object-store request in this diff scales with records, shards, partitions or indices; list is the only fan-out and it is now countable. Three major findings remain, all forward-facing onto M1.2/M1.3 rather than defects in what runs today: readFully is the only way to enforce Body.length and it instructs backends to materialise the whole object, which is the constraint the class javadoc claims to enforce; the key-limit case probes only the refusal above the advertised limit, so the very scenario its comment names (advertise 1024, reject at 255) still passes; and the SPI shape overturns two things research doc 07 states verbatim with no ADR and no revision banner, which the adr skill makes required and same-commit.

findings.title: readFully is the only way to enforce length, and its javadoc tells every backend to materialise the whole object -- the constraint the same class claims to enforce
findings.failure_scenario: Body's class javadoc says 'Never a byte[] ... Constraint C8 -- nothing materialises a whole object in heap -- is enforced at the SPI BOUNDARY rather than by convention: if the interface cannot express a full-buffer write, nobody can accidentally perform one.' Line 40 then adds `public byte[] readFully()` and line 38 instructs 'Backends call this rather than reading the stream themselves.' The interface now expresses a full-buffer write, so the sentence above it is false as written. It is also the ONLY length enforcement available: Body offers no validating stream, so a backend that streams (Files.copy on M1.2's LocalFsBinStore, RequestBody.fromInputStream(in, len) on the eventual S3 backend -- both of which take a length and never need the array) has to choose between honouring the F4 fix and honouring C8. The M1.2 author reading line 38 takes the instruction: `Files.write(tmp, body.readFully())` instead of `Files.copy(body.open().get(), tmp)`. Quantified consequence against docs/research/40-implementation/02-streaming-io-and-memory.md section 7: the budget allows 'In-flight PUT buffers <= 50 x 8 MiB = 400 MiB, counted in the pool'; readFully allocates a heap byte[] per in-flight PUT OUTSIDE that pool, so 50 concurrent segment PUTs add an unaccounted 400 MiB, and the flatness soak that section calls 'the acceptance criterion for constraint C8' fails -- as does M1 acceptance criterion 8 (a 200 MB body under a 256 MB heap) the moment anything larger than a commit delta goes through a real backend. Fix: give Body a length-checking FilterInputStream (`Body.checkedStream()` that throws IOException at EOF when the count differs, and on overrun as soon as it exceeds), keep readFully for MemoryBinStore and the small-control-record path, and narrow line 38 to say which backends may call it. That preserves the F4 fix -- a lying Body is still refused before anything is committed -- without making materialisation the sanctioned shape.

findings.title: The key-limit case probes only max+1; a backend that advertises 1024 and rejects at 255 passes it, which is the exact scenario its own comment claims to close
findings.failure_scenario: The comment says 'PROBED, not taken on advertisement. isPositive() is an assume: the longest key any other case writes is 7 bytes, so a backend with a real per-component limit passes while claiming 1024.' The test then asserts only that max+1 is REFUSED. Refusing max+1 is also what a backend that refuses everything over 255 does, so the diagnosis is right and the probe closes the other half of the hole. Nothing in the suite writes a key longer than 13 bytes ('never-existed'), so the advertised limit is still never exercised. Concrete failure, and it is the next task: M1.2's LocalFsBinStore maps a key to a path, and a single path component over 255 bytes fails ENAMETOOLONG on ext4/xfs/tmpfs. Copying MemoryBinStore's `MAX_KEY_BYTES = 1024` into it -- the natural move, since the conformance suite is the contract -- yields a backend that passes every case in this class and then refuses real keys, which are long BY DESIGN: ADR-0003 puts a base64url tagged bloom filter in the object key (docs/research/30-design-space/02-partition-bloom-in-key.md section 7), so keys grow toward the limit as index count grows and the failure appears at scale, not in dev. docs/research/30-design-space/07-pluggable-store-abstraction.md section 3 names the missing case verbatim: 'Keys of exactly 1,024 bytes, and every character our key generator can emit, round-trip.' Fix is two lines in the same test: write a key of exactly `maxKeyBytes` (built from the characters the key generator emits -- base64url plus '/'), then get it back and assert the bytes, before the max+1 refusal. The pair is what makes the limit a probed fact rather than an advertisement.

findings.title: The SPI shape overturns two things research doc 07 states verbatim, with no ADR and no revision banner on the doc
findings.failure_scenario: docs/research/30-design-space/07-pluggable-store-abstraction.md section 1 is the SPI of record -- its own header says 'Read this if: you are defining the store interface or writing a backend' -- and it specifies `Stream<ObjectStat> list(String prefix, String startAfter); // lazily paged` and `record ObjectStat(String key, long size, Version version, long lastModifiedMillis)`. This diff reverses both, and section 3 of that same doc still requires the conformance case 'list is lexicographic, honours startAfter, and pages LAZILY WITHOUT BUFFERING ALL KEYS' -- a requirement the ListPage javadoc now argues is precisely the R9 defect. The arguments for both reversals are good and I would keep them; they are recorded only in javadoc, which nobody reading doc 07 sees. The adr skill fires twice here and says required, not optional: 'It changes a wire format or the store SPI. Required, not optional, and it travels in the same commit as the change' and 'It overturns a research conclusion ... Also add a warning revision banner to the affected research document.' AGENTS.md makes the corpus upstream of the product docs and says the banner wins over the earlier conclusion -- there is no banner, and grep over docs/internal/product/decisions/ finds no ADR mentioning the store SPI shape. Concrete failure: the M1.2/M1.3 author routes to doc 07 (it is the routing target for 'writing a backend'), implements against `Stream<ObjectStat>` and `lastModifiedMillis`, and finds out at compile time -- cheap. The expensive one is section 3's laziness requirement, which reads today as an unmet conformance obligation, so the next author writing the missing case can 'fix' the SPI back toward the shape F2 was raised to kill, with doc 07 as the citation. This is also the answer to the ObjectStat/lastModifiedMillis question: the javadoc argument is sound but it is in the wrong place. One ADR ('the store SPI pages explicitly and carries no mtime') with the rejected alternatives -- lazy Stream, mtime-carrying ObjectStat -- and their numbers (the meter under-reporting by four orders of magnitude; mtime precision and copy semantics differing per provider), plus a revision banner on doc 07 sections 1 and 3, discharges it.

findings.title: delete takes an unbounded List and its javadoc claims one request; the meter will count one where the backend issues many
findings.failure_scenario: 'Delete in one request where the backend supports it' cannot hold: S3 DeleteObjects caps at 1000 keys and errors above it, Azure Blob Batch caps at 256 sub-requests each accounted separately, and GCS has no true multi-object delete. So one call is 1, ceil(n/1000) or n requests depending on the backend, and M1.3's CountingBinStore -- which sees only the call and Capabilities -- records 1. That is the same shape as F2, and Capabilities already carries maxKeyBytes and minPartSize for exactly this purpose but no maxDeleteKeys; the F6 argument applies verbatim (adding a record component later is a canonical-constructor change, not an addition). Filed MINOR rather than major on three honest grounds: DELETE is free on S3, GCS and Azure so there is no dollar impact, the runaway is a per-prefix rate-limit event rather than a bill; GC and compaction are explicitly out of M1 scope so no caller exists yet; and unlike list, the meter is not blind -- it can count keys.size() as an upper bound. Worth a backlog row against M1.3 so the meter's delete count is decided rather than defaulted.

findings.title: maxKeys <= 0 is unspecified on the interface and misbehaves in the backend
findings.failure_scenario: `if (page.size() == maxKeys) { next = page.get(page.size() - 1).key(); }` with maxKeys == 0 evaluates page.get(-1) and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException -- an unchecked exception out of a method whose whole contract is that failures are checked. With maxKeys negative the equality never holds and the call returns the ENTIRE listing in one page, unbounded, which is the buffering ListPage exists to prevent. The interface javadoc says only 'upper bound on this page; the backend may return fewer', so neither behaviour is a contract violation today and neither is reachable from M1 code. It becomes reachable at M1.3b, where a LIST governor naturally passes a remaining budget that can reach zero. Either state the precondition on line 74 and validate it, or define maxKeys <= 0 as an empty page with the resume point unchanged.

findings.title: minPartSize and batchDelete are decorative in the same way Body.length was
findings.failure_scenario: F4's argument was that an unenforced component is worse than none because something downstream believes it. minPartSize describes multipart, which the BinStore javadoc says is explicitly out of M1 ('no multipart ... arrives with the real segment format in M2'), and nothing reads or probes it; batchDelete is advertised true by MemoryBinStore and no conformance case constrains it, so a backend looping per key advertises the same value as one that batches. Only conditionalWrites and maxKeyBytes are asserted (lines 328-334), and only conditionalWrites is asserted in a form that would fail if it were a lie -- the concurrent putIfAbsent case. Not blocking: the CostTable reasoning (a component added later is a signature change) justifies carrying minPartSize now. Worth a row so M1.3 either probes them or drops them.

findings.title: The concurrency case hangs rather than fails when a backend does not reach the barrier
findings.failure_scenario: `start.await()` has no timeout and `pool.invokeAll(tasks)` has none either. Parties (16) equals pool size (16), so it is sound for MemoryBinStore. A future backend whose putIfAbsent blocks -- M1.2's O_CREAT|O_EXCL against a held lock, or a MinIO fixture that stalls -- or any environment where the executor cannot run all 16 concurrently turns the highest-value case in the suite into an indefinite hang in the L1 tier, which reads as a lost session rather than a red test. `start.await(5, SECONDS)` and `invokeAll(tasks, 30, SECONDS)` make the same case fail loudly. Also, `startsWith("writer-")` accepts any blend whose first 7 bytes come from any writer; asserting the stored body equals one of the 16 candidate bodies exactly is the stronger form and costs a Set.contains.
